note.note:
History:
- Presenting complaint: 5 days of dry cough and continuous runny nose.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began ~5 days ago; cough described as dry, occurring about every 20–30 minutes; nasal discharge ongoing and described as green.
- Associated symptoms: Subjective feverishness (feels hot to touch and intermittently chilled), myalgias/aching muscles; brief diarrhoea around onset that resolved; no measured temperature recorded.
- Respiratory symptoms negatives: No sputum production, no haemoptysis, no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no pleuritic pain.
- Other context: Partial symptomatic relief with lemon/“Lemsip” (taken 2–3 times/day at start and end of day); no other self-treatments recorded.

Past Medical History:
- Diabetes mellitus (type not specified).
- Hypertension.
- Allergies: Seasonal hay fever (history). No known drug allergies reported.
- Current medications: Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented; Lisinopril — dose/route/frequency not documented (patient stated “two hundred” when asked about dose; accuracy unclear).
- Prior hospitalizations: Not recorded.
- Social: Lives with partner and a dog; works as an office manager; alcohol: “the odd cherry” (unclear frequency); smoking status: Not recorded.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded (no measured temperature, heart rate, BP, respiratory rate, or SpO2 documented).
- Reported/observed findings from history:
  - Patient appears to have no respiratory distress (per history).
  - Dry cough every ~20–30 minutes.
  - Continuous green nasal discharge.
  - Subjective feverishness (hot to touch) and intermittent chills.
  - Myalgias/aches.
  - Eating and drinking normally; passing urine normally.
  - Height 5'5"; weight 65 kg (patient-reported).
- Relevant negatives: No throat swelling reported; no vomiting or ongoing diarrhea; no headache or vision change; no focal sinus pain recorded.
- Formal physical exam findings: Not recorded.

Impression:
- Most likely diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory tract infection (probable viral chest/URTI) causing dry cough and rhinorrhea.
- Additional plausible considerations consistent with the transcript:
  - Acute bronchitis (viral) — prominent dry cough following URTI symptoms; possible but likely viral and self-limited.
  - ACE inhibitor (lisinopril)–related cough — possible contributor given medication use, but less likely as new acute onset is temporally linked to URTI.
- (DDx and transcript largely consistent regarding likely viral cause. Conflict noted: DDx comments that the lisinopril dose was reported incorrectly; transcript records the patient stating “two hundred” when asked about lisinopril dose.)

Management Plan:
- Immediate/advice given during consultation:
  - Obtain an oral thermometer and check temperature regularly.
  - Continue symptomatic measures (Lemsip/lemons) but avoid taking additional paracetamol-containing products concurrently with Lemsip (Lemsip contains paracetamol).
  - Use cough syrup only at night if coughing prevents sleep; avoid routine daytime suppression of cough.
  - Monitor symptoms closely given diabetes (higher risk of bacterial infection/complication).
- Escalation criteria requiring re-contact or review:
  - Persistent or recurrent temperature >37.5–38°C (doctor advised to check and re-contact if ongoing fever).
  - Worsening cough, new/ increasing sputum production, haemoptysis, new shortness of breath, or chest pain.
  - If symptoms do not settle or worsen, clinician may consider antibiotics (not started now).
- Routine health maintenance:
  - Ensure regular diabetes and blood pressure follow-up with GP; patient advised to continue routine monitoring.
  - If not already provided, obtain blood glucose monitoring equipment per usual diabetes care (patient reported not having one at home).

Patient Summary:
- Patient presented with a 5-day history of dry cough and green rhinorrhea with subjective feverishness and myalgias, likely representing a viral upper respiratory tract infection (possible acute bronchitic component). Symptomatic treatment advised, thermometer recommended, and instructions given to re-contact if fever persists/worsens or if respiratory symptoms progress; antibiotics only if clinical course suggests bacterial infection.

Key Takeaways:
- Get a thermometer and monitor temperature; re-contact if fever persists or is high.
- Continue symptomatic measures (Lemsip)—do not take additional paracetamol-containing products simultaneously.
- Seek urgent care or contact clinician if increased breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, or marked worsening of symptoms.

Next Steps:
- Patient to obtain and use a thermometer; monitor and record temperatures.
- If fever >37.5–38°C or persistent/worsening symptoms, contact clinician/GP for reassessment (possible consideration of antibiotics if bacterial infection suspected).
- Maintain routine diabetes and hypertension follow-up with GP; consider obtaining home blood glucose monitoring if appropriate.
- No tests or imaging were ordered during this consultation.

Quality checks:
- Missing but expected elements: objective vital signs (temperature, pulse, BP, respiratory rate, SpO2), formal physical examination findings (lung auscultation), smoking status, medication doses/administration details, any COVID-19/influenza testing status.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: DDx states the lisinopril dose was reported incorrectly; transcript records the patient stating “two hundred” when asked about lisinopril dose — conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Mostly clear; some brief disfluencies and unclear numeric detail regarding lisinopril dose. Overall adequate for clinical assessment.
